title: The Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol for Tea Efflux Appliances (HTCPCP-TEA)
summary: This is an April 1st joke RFC. It extends the humorous Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol so networked pots can brew tea in all its variety. It is not a serious specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st joke extends a coffee-pot control protocol to networked tea appliances. It defines a way to list tea varieties and request one.

questions: what is the hyper text coffee pot control protocol
what is the message/teapot media type
how do you brew tea over http
subtitle: An April 1st joke extends the coffee-pot control protocol to tea appliances.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke says the Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol has no way to brew tea.
tldr.mechanism: It proposes tea-specific BREW requests, a message/teapot media type, tea variety URIs and related responses.
tldr.outcome: This humorous document updates RFC 2324; its protocol additions are presented as a joke.

today: RFC 7168 is an Informational April 1st joke document that updates RFC 2324. It is humor, not a serious protocol proposal.

sections.title: Tea and the Coffee-Pot Protocol
sections.content:
RFC 7168 is an April 1st joke document. It extends the Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol (HTCPCP) because, as the RFC puts it, the base specification does not allow networked teapots to make tea.

The extension describes requests and responses for tea-producing devices. The unit metadata records that it updates RFC 2324.
sections.plainLanguage: This April 1st document jokes that a coffee-pot protocol needs a tea extension. It describes requests to networked tea appliances.

sections.title: Selecting and Brewing a Tea
sections.content:
A client sends a BREW request. For a request to the / URI with content type message/teapot, the pot does not begin brewing; it returns an Alternates header listing tea varieties and their URIs. A client must check that list and use a specific URI in a later request.

For a selected variety, the pot follows the base HTCPCP specification. The RFC recommends that clients send another BREW request with the body stop to end brewing; an early stop requires the pot to abort and serve the weaker result.
sections.plainLanguage: The first request asks which teas are available. The client then selects a URI and can send stop to end brewing.

sections.title: Media Type and Response Codes
sections.content:
The extension defines the message/teapot media type for tea requests. It updates Accept-Additions to include Sugar, Xylitol and Stevia as sugar-type values.

The RFC recommends response code 300 for a request that returns tea choices without starting to brew. A service may use 403 for an additions combination it considers contrary to drinkers' consensus. A pot not provisioned to brew coffee may return 503 for temporary unavailability or 418 to indicate it is a teapot.
sections.plainLanguage: The request uses message/teapot to ask for tea. The RFC also describes responses for choices, rejected additions and a pot that does not make coffee.
